items.title: Salient Features of the Indian Constitution
items.body:
## In one line

The salient features are the defining characteristics of the Constitution — written and lengthy, federal yet unitary, and parliamentary.

## Why it is asked

'Which is or is not a feature' and the current Article, Part and Schedule counts recur every year.

## Core features

- **Lengthiest written constitution** in the world — originally 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules (1949); now about **470 Articles, 25 Parts, 12 Schedules**. Its bulk owes to the country's diversity, the influence of the **Government of India Act, 1935**, a single constitution for centre and states, and the role of legal experts.
- **Drawn from various sources** but tailored to Indian conditions (see the borrowed-sources note).
- **Blend of rigidity and flexibility** — Article 368 provides amendment by **special majority** and by **special majority + ratification by half the states**, while some provisions change by **simple majority**.
- **Federal system with unitary bias** — K.C. Wheare called it a **'quasi-federation'**. Article 1 calls India a **'Union of States'**: the federation is not an agreement of states and **no state can secede**. The word 'Federation' is never used.
- **Parliamentary (Westminster) government** at the centre and states, chosen over the US presidential system; but the **Indian Parliament is not sovereign** (laws face judicial review).
- **Synthesis of parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy** — Article 21 uses **'procedure established by law'** (not 'due process'); Parliament amends the Constitution, the Supreme Court exercises judicial review.
- **Single citizenship** despite a dual polity — one Indian citizenship for all (British model), unlike the US dual citizenship.
- **Universal adult franchise** (Art 326); voting age lowered from 21 to **18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988**.
- **Integrated and independent judiciary**, **independent bodies** (EC, CAG, UPSC, SPSC), and a **three-tier government** (73rd/74th Amendments, 1992).
- **A secular state** — positive secularism giving equal respect to all religions.

## Terms explained

- **Quasi-federation** — federal in form but with a strong tilt towards the Centre (K.C. Wheare’s term).
- **‘Procedure established by law’** — a person’s liberty can be taken only by a set legal procedure (narrower than the American ‘due process’).
- **Universal adult franchise** — every adult citizen’s right to vote, regardless of wealth or education.
- **Single citizenship** — one national citizenship for all Indians, unlike the dual citizenship of the United States.

## TL;DR

- Lengthiest written constitution: original 395 Articles/22 Parts/8 Schedules (1949); now about 470/25/12.
- Blend of rigidity and flexibility via Article 368: simple, special, and special-plus-state-ratification amendments.
- Quasi-federal (K.C. Wheare); Article 1 = 'Union of States' — no secession, not an agreement of states; word 'Federation' never used.
- Parliamentary (Westminster) system adopted; Indian Parliament is NOT sovereign (unlike Britain).
- Single citizenship (British model) despite a dual polity; universal adult franchise under Art 326, age 18 via 61st Amendment (1988).

items.title: Sources Borrowed from Other Constitutions
items.body:
## In one line

A ready-reference of which feature of the Constitution was borrowed from which country.

## Why it is asked

Source-matching is among the most repeated objective questions.

## Country-to-feature map

| Source | Features borrowed |
|---|---|
| **British** | Parliamentary government, rule of law, bicameralism, cabinet system, single citizenship, prerogative writs |
| **US** | Fundamental Rights, independence of judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of President, removal of judges, VP's post |
| **Irish** | Directive Principles of State Policy, method of President's election, nomination of Rajya Sabha members |
| **Soviet (USSR)** | Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble |
| **Canadian** | Strong-centre federation, residuary powers with the centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of SC |
| **Australian** | Concurrent List, joint sitting of Parliament, freedom of trade and commerce |
| **Weimar (Germany)** | Emergency provisions for suspension of Fundamental Rights |
| **French** | Republic; ideals of Liberty, Equality, Fraternity |
| **Japanese** | Procedure established by law (Art 21) |
| **GoI Act, 1935** | Federal scheme, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, office of Governor, emergency provisions |
| **South African** | Amendment procedure, election of Rajya Sabha members |

- Borrowed features were **adapted** to Indian conditions — for example, the cabinet system does not carry the same supremacy as in the UK.

## Terms explained

- **Writs** — formal court orders (such as Habeas Corpus) used to protect rights, borrowed from Britain.
- **DPSP (Directive Principles of State Policy)** — guidelines the State should follow, borrowed from Ireland.
- **Concurrent List** — subjects on which both the Centre and the states may legislate, borrowed from Australia.

## TL;DR

- British: parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, writs.
- US: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, VP's post.
- Irish: Directive Principles of State Policy; Soviet/USSR: Fundamental Duties.
- Canadian: strong-centre federation and residuary powers; Australian: Concurrent List and joint sitting.
- Weimar (Germany): suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency; GoI Act 1935: federal scheme and emergency provisions.
keyPoints: British: parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, writs.
US: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, VP's post.
Irish: Directive Principles of State Policy; Soviet/USSR: Fundamental Duties.
Canadian: strong-centre federation and residuary powers; Australian: Concurrent List and joint sitting.
Weimar (Germany): suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency; GoI Act 1935: federal scheme and emergency provisions.
items.mnemonic: DPSP = Ireland's gift; Duties = the USSR's; Emergency FR-suspension = Germany's Weimar.

items.title: The Preamble — Text, Components & 42nd Amendment
items.body:
## In one line

The Preamble is the short opening statement of the Constitution that declares its ideals and the source of its authority (the people of India).

## Why it is asked

Its exact words, the 42nd Amendment additions and the link to the Objectives Resolution are standard questions.

## What the Preamble is

- The **introductory statement** to the Constitution, outlining its **guiding principles and philosophy**. It is based on the **Objectives Resolution** moved by **Jawaharlal Nehru** and adopted by the Constituent Assembly.

## Four components

1. **Source of authority** — 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA'; the Constitution derives its authority from the people.
2. **Nature of the state** — Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
3. **Objectives** — Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
4. **Date of adoption** — 26 November 1949.

## The 42nd Amendment (1976)

- The Preamble has been amended **only once** — the 42nd Amendment added **'Socialist'** and **'Secular'** to the state's description and **'and integrity'** to 'unity of the nation'.

## Keyword sources

| Term | Borrowed from |
|---|---|
| We, the people of India | USA |
| Justice | Russian Revolution / USA |
| Liberty | French Revolution / USA |
| Equality, Fraternity | French Revolution |

- Scholars' praise: **K.M. Munshi** — 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'; **Thakur Das Bhargava** — 'soul of the Constitution'; **Ernest Barker** — 'key-note to the Constitution'.

## Terms explained

- **Preamble** — the short opening declaration that states the ideals of the Constitution and that its authority comes from the people.
- **Objectives Resolution** — Nehru’s statement of aims on which the Preamble is based.
- **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic** — independent of outside control; aiming at social-economic equality; equal respect for all religions; ruled by elected representatives; with an elected (not hereditary) head of state.

## TL;DR

- Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru.
- Four components: source of authority (We the People), nature of state, objectives, date (26 Nov 1949).
- Keywords describing the state: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
- Objectives: Justice (social/economic/political), Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
- Amended only once — 42nd Amendment (1976) added Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

items.title: Status of the Preamble — Key Cases
items.body:
## In one line

This traces, through court cases, whether the Preamble is actually part of the Constitution and whether it can be amended.

## Why it is asked

The Berubari to Kesavananda to LIC case ladder is tested often.

## Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution?

| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Berubari Union** | 1960 | Preamble is the 'key to open the mind of the makers' but **NOT a part** of the Constitution; not enforceable. |
| **Kesavananda Bharati** | 1973 | Preamble **IS a part** of the Constitution and can be amended (subject to the basic structure). |
| **Union Govt v. LIC of India** | 1995 | Reaffirmed the Preamble is **an integral part**, but is **not directly enforceable** in a court. |

## Takeaways

- The Preamble **can be amended** under Article 368, but its **basic features cannot be destroyed**.
- It is **not a source of power** nor a limitation on powers, and it is **non-justiciable** (not enforceable by courts).

## Don't confuse

'**Part of the Constitution**' and '**enforceable**' are not the same thing. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the Preamble **is a part** of the Constitution, but no court enforces the Preamble by itself — it only helps interpret other provisions.

## Terms explained

- **Justiciable / non-justiciable** — enforceable in a court versus not enforceable by itself.
- **Basic structure** — the Constitution’s core features that even an amendment cannot destroy.
- **‘Part of the Constitution’ vs ‘enforceable’** — being a part means it can guide interpretation; being enforceable would mean a court could act on it directly. The Preamble is a part but not enforceable on its own.

## TL;DR

- Berubari (1960): Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution and not enforceable.
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Preamble IS part of the Constitution and is amendable.
- LIC of India (1995): Preamble is an integral part but not directly enforceable.
- The Preamble can be amended under Art 368 but its basic features cannot be destroyed.
- The Preamble is non-justiciable — not enforceable in a court of law.

Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Preamble IS part of the Constitution and is amendable.
LIC of India (1995): Preamble is an integral part but not directly enforceable.
The Preamble can be amended under Art 368 but its basic features cannot be destroyed.
The Preamble is non-justiciable — not enforceable in a court of law.

items.title: Parts of the Constitution — Quick Reference
items.body:
## In one line

A quick map of the Constitution's Parts and which Articles each Part covers.

## Why it is asked

'Which Part deals with X' is a reliable one-mark question.

## Key Parts and their Articles

| Part | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| I | The Union and its Territory | 1-4 |
| II | Citizenship | 5-11 |
| III | Fundamental Rights | 12-35 |
| IV | Directive Principles (DPSP) | 36-51 |
| IVA | Fundamental Duties | 51A |
| V | The Union (Executive/Legislature/Judiciary) | 52-151 |
| VI | The States | 152-237 |
| IX | The Panchayats | 243-243O |
| IXA | The Municipalities | 243P-243ZG |
| IXB | Co-operative Societies | 243ZH-243ZT |
| XI | Union-State Relations | 245-263 |
| XIVA | Tribunals | 323A-323B |
| XVIII | Emergency Provisions | 352-360 |
| XX | Amendment of the Constitution | 368 |

- **Parts added later**: IXA & IXB (73rd/74th & 97th Amendments), XIVA (42nd Amendment). Part VII was **repealed** by the 7th Amendment.
- The document was **handwritten** (Hindi and English), drafted in **2 years, 11 months, 18 days**, adopted **26 Nov 1949**, enforced **26 Jan 1950**.

## Terms explained

- **Part** — a numbered division of the Constitution that groups related Articles together.
- **Article** — a single numbered provision of the Constitution.
- **Repealed** — formally removed or cancelled (as Part VII was by the 7th Amendment).

## TL;DR

- Part III = Fundamental Rights (12-35); Part IV = DPSP (36-51); Part IVA = Fundamental Duties (51A).
- Part IX = Panchayats, IXA = Municipalities, IXB = Co-operative Societies.
- Part XIVA = Tribunals (added by 42nd Amendment); Part VII repealed by 7th Amendment.
- Part XVIII = Emergency Provisions (352-360); Part XX = Amendment (Art 368).
- Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950; drafted in 2 years 11 months 18 days.

items.title: Schedules of the Constitution — Quick Reference
items.body:
## In one line

A quick map of the twelve Schedules and the subject each one lists.

## Why it is asked

Schedule-matching (anti-defection, official languages, panchayats) is a repeat favourite.

## The 12 Schedules

| Schedule | Subject |
|---|---|
| First | States and Union Territories |
| Second | Salaries of officials (President, Governors, Judges, etc.) |
| Third | Forms of oaths and affirmations |
| Fourth | Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha |
| Fifth | Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes |
| Sixth | Administration of Tribal Areas (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) |
| **Seventh** | Union, State and Concurrent Lists (division of powers) |
| **Eighth** | 22 official languages |
| **Ninth** | Land reform laws (protected under Art 31-B) |
| **Tenth** | Anti-Defection Law |
| **Eleventh** | Powers of Panchayats (Art 243-G) |
| **Twelfth** | Powers of Municipalities (Art 243-W) |

## Amendment origins

- **9th Schedule** — added by the **1st Amendment, 1951** (shield land-reform laws from judicial review).
- **10th Schedule** — added by the **52nd Amendment, 1985** (Anti-Defection).
- **11th & 12th Schedules** — added by the **73rd & 74th Amendments, 1992**.
- The Constitution began with **8 Schedules**; the concept was first seen in the **GoI Act, 1935** (10 schedules).

## Terms explained

- **Schedule** — an appendix at the end of the Constitution that lists details such as languages, salaries or the three legislative lists.
- **Anti-Defection Law** — rules (Tenth Schedule) that disqualify a legislator who defects from the party on whose ticket they were elected.
- **Ninth Schedule** — a list of laws (mostly land reform) placed beyond ordinary court challenge.

## TL;DR

- 7th Schedule = Union/State/Concurrent Lists; 8th Schedule = 22 official languages.
- 9th Schedule = land reform laws (Art 31-B), added by 1st Amendment (1951).
- 10th Schedule = Anti-Defection Law, added by 52nd Amendment (1985).
- 11th (Panchayats) and 12th (Municipalities) Schedules added by 73rd/74th Amendments (1992).
- Original Constitution had 8 Schedules; now 12.
keyPoints: 7th Schedule = Union/State/Concurrent Lists; 8th Schedule = 22 official languages.
9th Schedule = land reform laws (Art 31-B), added by 1st Amendment (1951).
10th Schedule = Anti-Defection Law, added by 52nd Amendment (1985).
11th (Panchayats) and 12th (Municipalities) Schedules added by 73rd/74th Amendments (1992).
Original Constitution had 8 Schedules; now 12.

items.title: Exam-Precision: Preamble Liberties, Welfare State & Limited Government
items.body:
## In one line

The precise Preamble wording and the idea of limited (constitutional) government that papers have asked exactly.

## Why it is asked

Distractors such as 'economic liberty' are deliberately planted here.

## Which 'Liberty' does the Preamble grant?

The Preamble secures **Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship**. It does **NOT** mention **'economic liberty'** - a favourite UPSC distractor. (Economic content enters through *Justice*, not *Liberty*.)

| Preamble word | Exact scope |
|---|---|
| **Justice** | social, **economic** and political |
| **Liberty** | thought, expression, belief, faith, worship |
| **Equality** | of status and of opportunity |
| **Fraternity** | dignity of the individual; unity and integrity of the nation |

## Where objectives are echoed elsewhere

- **Economic Justice** as an objective is provided in **both the Preamble AND the Directive Principles of State Policy** (Part IV, esp. Arts 38-39).
- The ideal of a **Welfare State** is enshrined in the **Directive Principles of State Policy** (not the Preamble or Fundamental Rights).
- **UDHR (1948)** ideals are reflected in the **Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties**.
- The Fundamental Duty to 'uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India' is in **Article 51A (Part IVA)**, not the Preamble.

## Constitutional (limited) government

- A **constitutional government** places **restrictions on the authority of the State in the interest of individual liberty** - that is, limited government. It is the opposite of restricting individual liberty in favour of State authority.
- **How India differs from Britain**: the British Parliament is **sovereign/supreme**, but the **Indian Parliament's power to legislate is limited** by a written Constitution and judicial review.

## Terms explained

- **Liberty in the Preamble** — freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; it does not include ‘economic liberty’.
- **Welfare state** — a state that promotes citizens’ well-being; this ideal sits in the Directive Principles, not the Preamble.
- **Constitutional (limited) government** — a government whose power over citizens is restricted in favour of individual liberty.
- **UDHR (1948)** — the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, whose ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.

## TL;DR

- Preamble grants Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship - NOT 'economic liberty'.
- Economic Justice as an objective is provided in both the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy.
- The ideal of a Welfare State is enshrined in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
- UDHR (1948) ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.
- A constitutional (limited) government restricts the State's authority in favour of individual liberty.
keyPoints: Preamble grants Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship - NOT 'economic liberty'.
Economic Justice as an objective is provided in both the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy.
The ideal of a Welfare State is enshrined in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
UDHR (1948) ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.
A constitutional (limited) government restricts the State's authority in favour of individual liberty.
The British Parliament is sovereign, but the Indian Parliament's legislative power is limited by judicial review and a written Constitution.

items.title: For Mains — Salient Features & the Preamble
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance)

This theme (clauses M3-1 and M3-15a) is examined as **analysis of design choices**, not fact-recall. The two hot sub-themes are (a) the Preamble as the Constitution's philosophy and whether it binds, and (b) the quasi-federal balance.

| Dimension | Points to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Features** | Lengthiest written; quasi-federal (Art 1 'Union of States'); parliamentary but not sovereign; blend of rigidity/flexibility (Art 368); single citizenship; integrated judiciary |
| **Significance of Preamble** | Declares source, nature, objectives, date; aid to interpretation; 'identity card' / 'soul' of the Constitution |
| **Judicial evolution** | Berubari (1960) not part → Kesavananda (1973) part & amendable within basic structure → LIC (1995) integral but non-justiciable |
| **Criticism / tension** | 'Secular/Socialist' added by 42nd Amendment (1976) debated; quasi-federal centralisation vs. state autonomy; welfare promise vs. non-justiciable DPSP |
| **Way forward** | Cooperative federalism (GST Council, Inter-State Council); 'living constitution' reading |

**Data / authorities to quote:** K.M. Munshi ('horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'); Thakur Das Bhargava ('soul of the Constitution'); N.A. Palkhivala ('identity card of the Constitution'); Kesavananda Bharati (1973), S.R. Bommai (1994, secularism as basic structure), Berubari (1960), LIC (1995); K.C. Wheare's 'quasi-federation'; 106th Amendment (2023) as proof of a living document.

**AP angle:** Article 1's 'Union of States' and the centre's reorganisation power under Article 3 are exactly what enabled the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** (bifurcation) — a live illustration that states have no indestructible territory and that federalism in India is centre-tilted.

**Use in answers:** open an answer on the Preamble by quoting Palkhivala's 'identity card'; use the three-case ladder (Berubari → Kesavananda → LIC) as a crisp timeline; for federalism, cite S.R. Bommai and the Art 1/Art 3 point with the AP-2014 example; close by framing the Constitution as a 'living document' validated by 106 amendments. A simple Preamble-components diagram (source · nature · objectives · date) adds structure.
keyPoints: Lead Preamble answers with its four components and the 'soul/identity card' quotations.
Use the Berubari (1960) → Kesavananda (1973) → LIC (1995) ladder for the 'is it a part?' question.
Argue quasi-federalism via Art 1 'Union of States', centre-tilt features, and S.R. Bommai (1994).
Note the 42nd Amendment (1976) debate over adding Socialist/Secular; secularism is basic structure.
AP angle: Art 1/Art 3 reorganisation power underpins the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 (bifurcation).
Frame the Constitution as a living document — 106 amendments to date (106th, 2023).
